description:
\P[1]'s severed, decapitated head.  Thank's to \P[1]'s dragon blood, it is very much alive, talkative, and capable of making smart mouth wisecracks as ever.
Durable, even bounces when dropped and tossed.  You can also USE it like other inventory items to talk to it, if you think it knows something it's body doesn't.
name: Your Severed Head
note:
<cgmzdesc:
While nearly indestructible, you know it's weaknesses.  If for some reason it is no longer re-attachable to any neck of yours, you have to kill it, throw it away, and grow a new head to be complete again.

When you are decapitated but don't leave your head lying around, you carry it with you, which allows you to still talk to NPCs, mouth off, breath fire, and re-attach it when you want to, if it is re-attachable.

When your severed head has the bloody, exposed flesh (meat and bone showing) burned with acid, or damaged in a similar way, you cannot re-attach your head because that inside-flesh sponge and meat tissue has been damaged, so it won't reconnect and heal.

If the tissue isn't burned or melted by acid, or some other nasty stuff, but simply cut and severed, your half-dragon insides and skin can and will clot, heal, and reconnect if you push the flesh and severed parts together and hold it in place, thanks to your half-dragon magical nature.

(Other body parts of yours can do the same, all of your parts.)

(If a severed body part is also missing, left around someplace and you lost it, you have to find it to reconnect it.  If it is still living, which is normally the case, you have to get it back if you want to have that body part.  You can only grow a replacement if the lost part is killed, melted, etc., or otherwise no longer lives or exists.  Sorry, but your half-zarakite magic has these limitations, in your case at least.)

When your head gets re-attached, then heals so that it is no longer on loose (which it is at first, depending on how you do it), it doesn't leave any scar tissue, scabs, marks, or discoloration, or ANY sign of past damage on your PERFECT pure-white dragon skin, at all.  This is normal, for you at least.  Half-dragons and pure-blooded zarakite dragons are like this, regardless of their skin color (not all have pure white skin, but you do).
>

description: Used for development and debugging of this game.
name: Cheater's Stone
note: <cgmzencyclopediahide>

description:
In-game menu for difficulty settings, decapitation frequency and other battle settings, various other options, helpful info,
how to zoom the display, make the game full-screen and back again, game controls, how to quit the game, and more...
name: Game Manual
note:
<cgmzdesc:
You can read through it any time outside of battle, more or less.

If parts of the game are too hard for you, it has an option or two to make the game easier, if desired.  Combat can be switched from normal to easy mode, where your characters get one free additional action per turn, plus some other bonus stuff to the math and under-the-hood calculations during combat, with attacking, evading attacks, damage, and other fun stuff...

Also included is an easy-money cheat, which has less and less usefulness as the game progresses.  It is a simple, reusable cheat that instantly gives you 50\G whenever you want.  Simple.  The reason it is less useful later in the game is because prices go up as the game goes on, and eventually 50\G becomes so trivial that it gets slow, tedious, and less practical to add only 50\G at a time.  This simple cheat is allowed to work this way, for good reasons.  Hey, you shouldn't have the game hold your hand in baby steps for the ENTIRE game, come on!
>

description:
Game encyclopedia, includes Beastiary of enemies encountered and their strengths and weaknesses,
information on treasures, weapons, and gear, and more.
name: Encyclopedia
note:
<cgmzdesc:
You are reading it right now!

You can read through it any time outside of battle, more or less.

As you progress through the game, do stuff, and come across new places, new things, new creatures/monsters/people, new weapons, new magic spells, and more, stuff gets added to the encyclopedia in new entries.

Some entries have a LOT of information, such as entries on important, specific people, and monsters you might encounter, with their strengths, weaknesses, special powers and special attacks, background information of sorts, and more.  Some of this stuff can be fairly verbose.  The same sometimes goes for inventory items, spells, weapons, etc.  Much of it is definitely worth a read.  Reading certain entries might also be needed for getting past some parts of the game and-or understanding things that come up in gameplay, just so you know, plus a lot of work has gone into it.

The encyclopedia also has maps in it, depending on how far you are into the game.  If you get a new map of some kind, to navigate through some area, it will show up in this encyclopedia, from the encyclopedia's main menu.
>

description: Seasoned, fried potato crisps.  Wrapped in magi-seal plastic so they keep.
name: Potato Crisps
note:
<tjsMaxCount:500>
<tjsFoodPrice:5>
<cgmzdesc:
Food and drink items will increase Special Points when ingested, giving general nutrition, protein, and such to one who consumes it.  This means that most food and drink items are good at restoring a character's abilities to use special or innate powers or abilities, when those abilities depend on some sort of nutrition, or focus and concentration, or physical effort that can wear one out, or other biological reserves of their body's cells and-or tissues.  For magical creatures, this can also include natural innate magic.  Yes, this certainly includes \P[1] and his innate zarakite magics.

Aside from Special Points being restored, eating food and consuming drinks typically also restores small amounts of Hit Points, but usually far less than that of healing potions.

A few food items, but not many, also restore Magic Points, of the kind that combat mages, wizards, and witches use for casting spells.  Keep in mind that such magic is a very different magic than zarakite magic, and unlike zarakite magic is available to nearly any intelligent, sentient species, with study, training, and practice, and draws upon different sources than zarakite magic.  By comparison, zarakite magic is innate if one is a zarakite or half zarakite, and draws from inner biological and natural sources of one's self if they are a zarakite dragon, or their non-human dragon side if a half zarakite.  Zarakite magic and the magic associated with Magic Points are mostly independent of each other, which is why they aren't powered with the same point system or methods of being replenished when low.  Magic points are a pool of available magic of an arcane sort, while zarakite magic comes from a dragon's metabolism and nutrition that their body builds up and stores, replenished for the most part by digesting food.
>

description: Restores HP by ~50 points.  The actual amount varies.
name: Healing Potion, Petty
note:
<tjsMaxCount:500>
<cgmzdesc:
A bit of important stuff about healing and curative magic potions needs to be mentioned here.

The short version:  This game is a little different than other game of it's type, in that a playable character can NOT use a healing potion on a DIFFERENT character who is OTHER than themself in combat.  *NO.*  Again, NO WAY.  The exception is any that brings back a character from death or defeat.

I'll explain why.  Yes, this is now the more detailed version, getting into the "how" and "why" stuff, and what's realistic versus outright screwball and utter nonsense.  Okay, can you imagine a party of adventurers going through rooms of a dungeon, then getting attacked by monsters, and after one of the main player characters of the party gets wounded, they pull a magic healing potion out of their travel backpack and hold it out to one of their companions, and say: "Oh, I want to make sure I still get my own attack in against one of these monsters this combat turn, so in seeing that I'm wounded but don't want to use up my turn with this healing potion, could you please just drink this potion FOR ME, so that it goes down YOUR throat INSTEAD OF mine, and thanks to insane quack logic, makes MY wounds SOMEHOW heal up, and not any of yours?  I'd really appreciate that, thanks, as I just somehow can't be bothered to drink it myself..."!?  Okay, seriously, WTF?  This type of thing is the most realism-shattering immersion-down-the-toilet completely unthinkable nonsense I have EVER heard of in any sort of RPG or JRPG game anything like this - Does anyone else see the problem with this concept?  One character, who is wounded, but trying to swing a sword or other weapon at a monster, while rushing around the room of the dungeon dodging blows and trying to avoid getting hit by the monster at the same time, can't be bothered to drink their own darn potion and wants one of their companions to drink a potion out of the shared inventory FOR them, to supposedly heal their wounds and not their companion's wounds, when both characters are rushing around the room of the dungeon trading blows with monsters doing the same, trying to hit each other's enemies while trying to avoid being hit, etc.  Sorry, there's just too many problems with this.  If someone wants to be a meathead of an armchair critic of some sort and say "Oh, but they could be fighting and I could pour it down their throat for them, to heal them and not me..." then my rebuttal as a Dungeon Master is "Fine, so your buddy can't run around and swing his sword, or dodge the monsters' attacks either, and has to stand still so you can pour it down his throat, and he has to not spill it while also swallowing it, which means he has to carefully stand still, be target practice for the monsters, and can't fight while you, his companion use up your turn pouring it down his throat, so NEITHER of you get to fight this turn!  That's my ruling!  If he had swallowed his own friggin' potion, you could still fight, but now you two have BOTH used your turn up doing something that he could have just done himself!  Too late, neither of you get to fight now.  TOUGH."  Fortunately, this game simplifies things a bit by not allowing any silly crap like that and just has it so that all characters who want to benefit from a magic healing potion have to drink their own darn potion, thank you.

As for the exception that was mentioned, the exception doesn't break this type of sticking-to-logic-and-common-sense that this game uses for this sort of thing, and I'll explain why:  If someone is dead or defeated, they are lying on the floor of the dungeon in this scenario, in a pool of their own blood most likely, and a companion can then make sure the defeated party member is lying on their back, rolling them to face up if necessary, pinch their defeated companion's nose shut, open the mouth, and pour the magic potion down their throat, bringing them back to life.  Note that the defeated companion in this case isn't running around trading and dodging blows with opponents, so a friend of his CAN get to them and hopefully get a potion to go down their throat, the friend using up their own turn to do so.  Note that the defeated companion still doesn't get their own turn of course, as they were lying dead in a pool of their own blood to begin with, duh.  Now that's my own armchair critic argument, Ha!

Yes, realism now prevails!  At least a bit more than the silly alternative...
>
